what_was_built.membership: kb.membership, one row per (organisation, principal), with issuer/subject, nullable display_name and email, and exactly two states: active, deactivated. Written only through kb.create_membership(), kb.accept_invitation() and kb.deactivate_membership(); kb_app holds no INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on the table at all.
what_was_built.deactivation: kb.deactivate_membership() is the whole PostgreSQL half: actor check, close the row, revoke the gateway's own durable browser sessions, increment the policy revision and append the journal entry, all in one transaction. Then the provider is contacted. Then the answer is recorded in a second transaction.
what_was_built.group_versus_direct: kb.library_grant is untouched and still means 'this person, directly'. kb.access_group_grant means 'everybody in this group'. kb.effective_role() takes the union as a maximum and kb.effective_role_paths() reports the two kinds separately, so the A08 explanation can name which path is still holding.
what_was_built.policy_journal: kb.access_policy_journal is append-only: no write policy, no write privilege, no endpoint. Group changes are journalled by a database trigger rather than by the caller, so there is exactly one place a change can be recorded and no path that skips it.
what_was_built.invitations: kb.invitation plus kb.create_invitation / accept / withdraw / mark_notified. Nothing is sent: there is no transport, no mailer parameter and no network call on the path, and delivery_state leaves 'operator_pending' only when a named operator records that they told the person out of band.
what_was_built.admins: kb.organisation_admin with claim / add / remove. It carries no library role, and the last administrator cannot be removed — an organisation with none has no supported way back except a psql session.

acceptance.a_disabled_user_with_a_valid_jwt_is_refu: test_membership_gate.py — 8 tests. The grant row is still there, the group row is still there, the browser session is still cryptographically valid, and the principal matches zero rows in all 18 subject tables, is refused writes, and cannot grant anybody else. A RESTRICTIVE policy additionally covers the two tables whose own policy has an own-row branch that never consults a role (kb.library_grant, kb.use_record).
acceptance.a_direct_grant_after_group_removal_is_ex: test_groups_and_grants.py::test_removing_the_group_leaves_the_direct_grant_and_the_ui_says_so and its mirror test_removing_the_direct_grant_leaves_the_group_and_the_ui_says_so. AccessExplanation returns the surviving path with its kind, its role and the group it came from — not a boolean, and not a denial.
acceptance.an_admin_does_not_silently_get_private_l: test_admin_scope.py — 12 tests. The admin set table has no role column, an administrator reads no row of somebody else's library, cannot write into one, cannot grant themselves access and cannot enrol themselves in a group that grants access. Every negative has a positive control beside it, because a suite of denials also passes for a principal whose administration is simply broken.

central_invariant.mutation_tested: three mutations were injected and reverted, each caught. (1) Moving the provider step before the PostgreSQL commit in deactivate_member failed 6 tests, including the ordering observation itself. (2) Removing `WHERE kb.membership_allows(p_principal)` from kb.effective_role failed 6 tests, including test_every_subject_table_is_closed. (3) Deleting the two remaining RESTRICTIVE policies failed 3 tests. The tests are not vacuous.

second_invariant.claim: a group grant and a direct grant are different things, and a full membership deactivation closes every path
second_invariant.how_the_gate_is_built: Inside kb.effective_role(), not as eighteen parallel policies. Every policy in 0002 and 0003 reaches its answer through that one function, so a principal whose membership is closed resolves to no role anywhere. A RESTRICTIVE policy is added only for kb.library_grant and kb.use_record, whose policies have an own-row branch that never consults a role. test_membership_gate.py::test_every_subject_table_is_closed walks all eighteen tables and asserts zero rows, and test_only_the_own_row_tables_need_a_second_statement asserts the list is exactly those two, read out of pg_policies.
second_invariant.why_not_one_policy_per_table: The first version put a RESTRICTIVE policy on all eighteen tables. That made C09's shipped structural guard test_link_policies_never_consult_the_target_role fail, because it asserts every policy on kb.project_library_link consults a role. The only ways to satisfy both were to leave the link table ungated or to write an expression mentioning a role it does not need. Moving the gate into the authority function closes the same rows with fewer moving parts, leaves C09's invariant intact and untouched, and test_every_subject_table_is_closed is the proof that no table was left open.

checks.name: keycloak_session_revocation
checks.reason: There is no Keycloak in this environment — no JVM, no realm, and runtime-capabilities.json reports keycloak_real.available=false. KeycloakSessionRevoker is a real HTTP client against Keycloak's documented admin API (client_credentials for a service account holding realm-management/manage-users, then POST /admin/realms/{realm}/users/{subject}/logout) and NOTHING executes it. It is not a mock and is not presented as one: no test imports it, no code path in the product constructs it, and the test harness substitutes an explicitly-labelled observer that opens a second connection to the real database. Two things need a live realm to settle: that the token's `sub` is the admin API's user id under a default configuration, and that the provider actually reports success. Both remain pending E03. The half of A16 that says 'the next request is refused on membership' IS verified here, against real PostgreSQL; the half that says 'sessions are revoked' is not.

findings_for_the_next_owner.finding: kb.effective_role is SECURITY DEFINER and reads kb.library_grant, which has FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. The rules say a SECURITY DEFINER function running as the table owner is subject to the owner's forced policies, which would make the function's own SELECT recurse into the policy that calls it. In this environment it does not fail, because the test fixtures apply the migrations as the superuser `postgres`, and a superuser bypasses RLS by role rather than by policy. The production arrangement — the migration role is kb_schema_owner, which IS the table owner — was not exercised here and cannot be from a test that connects as postgres. The safe general rule, and the one C08 follows, is: any function a policy expression calls must be able to read the table it is called for. kb.effective_role passes that test only because the migration role is a superuser in this workspace.
findings_for_the_next_owner.action_taken: reported, not fixed — 0002 is outside this card's allowed paths, and the fix (the functions that back the policies must be owned by a role that bypasses, or the tables must not be FORCEd) is the single DDL owner's decision. C08's own tables are RLS-enabled and NOT forced, with the reason written into the migration.

findings_for_the_next_owner.finding: Re-confirmed from C09 and still open: kb.rule_action has no permissive policy at all, so it is default-deny under RLS, but 0002 also granted SELECT on all kb tables to kb_app. The combination is safe today only because there is no policy to be filtered by. This card adds nothing to that table.
findings_for_the_next_owner.action_taken: reported again, unchanged. Belongs to the owner of 0002.

findings_for_the_next_owner.finding: A finding produced by writing the tests: an organisation administrator who may add anybody to a group can add THEMSELVES, and a group grant then hands them everything that group holds. The policy now refuses a row whose subject is the caller (leaving is still allowed, because PostgreSQL evaluates only USING for a DELETE). Group GRANTS were separately narrowed to require manager on the target library, which matches ACCESS-MODEL section 2. Both halves are needed: membership without the grant check is 'make a group, grant it a library, add yourself', and the grant check without it lets every library manager in the company reshape any group.
findings_for_the_next_owner.action_taken: fixed in 0004 and asserted by test_admin_scope.py::test_an_admin_cannot_enter_a_group_that_grants_access with the positive control test_an_admin_who_manages_the_library_does_see_the_paths.

findings_for_the_next_owner.finding: A second one from writing the tests: the first guard let any organisation administrator read any principal's grant paths for any library. That is a map of the company — it reveals that a private library exists and that a named person manages it, to somebody who can never open it. The guard now requires the caller to already hold a role on that library, and the API answers `not_visible` rather than an empty list so a UI cannot mistake 'you may not look' for 'they have nothing'.
findings_for_the_next_owner.action_taken: fixed in 0004 and asserted in both layers by test_groups_and_grants.py::test_a_third_party_cannot_ask_about_somebody_elses_paths and test_admin_scope.py::test_the_admin_api_answers_without_describing_a_library_they_cannot_see.

findings_for_the_next_owner.finding: Both take a principal and no organisation, because a policy expression and a per-request fence have no organisation context. In v1 there is exactly one organisation per installation, so the direction is conservative: a principal deactivated anywhere is refused everywhere, and any policy change anywhere invalidates any request's revision. A second organisation would need the organisation threaded through both signatures, which touches every policy in 0002 and 0003 and belongs to the single DDL owner.
findings_for_the_next_owner.action_taken: stated in the migration rather than papered over; the RLS triggers and the definer functions that DO have an organisation use it.

findings_for_the_next_owner.where: migrations/0004_membership.sql, comment above CREATE TABLE membership
findings_for_the_next_owner.finding: A deactivated member is refused every subject table but can still read their own kb.membership row, which is what tells them they were blocked, when, and by whom. That is deliberate and it is the only row they keep. It also means the two RESTRICTIVE policies cannot simply be extended to the C08 tables without losing the explanation the UI needs.

The journal detail was first filtered by TYPE — carry scalars and short strings. A test with a provider dict containing {'token': '<a real bearer token>'} passed that filter, because the value is a short string. The journal is readable by an administrator and outlives the request, so the filter is now an allow-list of keys this code chose.
